data.title: Mis-selling starts with sales targets, not branch counters: RBI DG Murmu
data.description:
Mis-selling of financial products often stems from sales targets and variable pay structures rather than actions at the branch level, said S C Murmu, Deputy Governor of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). He urged financial institutions to examine whether their incentive structures reward sales volumes or customer outcomes and how these are measured.
 
“Look hard at incentives. Mis-selling rarely begins at the branch counter. It begins with a sales target and a variable pay scheme. Ask what your incentives actually reward: volumes or customer outcomes. And ask how you measure each,” Murmu said, speaking at an event in Mumbai.
 
Mis-selling has remained a concern across India's financial sector, particularly in the distribution of insurance policies, mutual funds and other third-party products through banks and financial institutions.
  
Murmu also highlighted the significant regulatory changes awaiting banks from April 1, 2027, when the new prudential framework is scheduled to come into effect. The transition will involve the introduction of expected credit loss (ECL)-based provisioning, implementation of the remaining Basel III standards and adoption of a new standardised approach to credit risk.
 
Under the ECL framework, banks will have to make provisions for losses they expect to incur rather than only for losses that have already materialised. The framework will replace the existing incurred-loss-based provisioning approach with a forward-looking model requiring banks to provide for potential credit losses earlier.
 
Under the new norms, banks will classify financial assets into three stages based on changes in credit risk and make provisions accordingly. Stage 1 assets will attract provisions for 12-month expected credit losses, while assets in Stages 2 and 3 will require provisions based on lifetime expected credit losses.
 
The changes will make the banking system more sensitive to risk and place greater responsibility on boards, Murmu said.
 
With the shift towards principle-based regulation, boards will have greater flexibility in determining their institutions' risk appetite. However, this will also increase their responsibility to define that appetite in both qualitative and quantitative terms and hold management accountable for adhering to it.
 
Murmu also highlighted the importance of investments in technology and people, saying these were no longer optional for financial institutions. Boards needed to understand how technology was being deployed and the risks associated with it.
 
He also pointed to changes in the RBI's governance directions for banks, which came into effect on October 1, 2026. The revised directions replaced checklist-based board agendas with principle-based guidance, doing away with a long list of prescribed routine agenda items. This would free up board time, which directors should use to focus more on strategy and risks, including technology-related risks, and ensure preparedness for the transition to the new prudential framework in April 2027, he said.
 
Murmu also called for closer coordination among financial sector regulators, given the overlap in their mandates. A listed bank, for instance, is subject to the RBI's prudential norms and related-party lending guidelines, as well as listing regulations governing related-party transactions.
 
Similarly, banks distribute insurance and mutual fund products, making mis-selling a concern across multiple regulators. Cyber resilience also requires common baseline standards, as a single incident could affect a bank, an insurer and a market infrastructure institution simultaneously.
 
“Regulation does not keep pace by writing rules faster. It keeps pace by being clearer about what it expects of those who run and oversee institutions, and then by trusting their judgement,” he said.

data.title: Beyond hospital beds: Bajaj bets on a new model of healthcare delivery
data.description:
At a time when India's leading hospital chains are expanding bed capacity and seeking higher revenue per occupied bed, the Bajaj Group is attempting to build a healthcare business with a different set of economics — one that relies less on hospitalisation and more on managing a patient's health over a lifetime.
 
Its healthcare venture, Bajaj Integrated Health System (BIHS), which unveiled its brand Nivara on Thursday, expects a substantial portion of its earnings to come from outside hospitals. All its doctors, including super-specialists, will be on its payroll without revenue-linked targets, while a proposed subscription-based managed care model seeks to align the interests of insurers, healthcare providers and patients.
 
 
“We believe that we are deriving profit from the lifetime value of that patient, or actually, the community,” Nirav Bajaj, managing director and chief executive officer of BIHS, told Business Standard. “Our intent is to keep you healthy and not benefit from when you are ailing,” he said.
 
The century-old conglomerate is committing ₹2,000-2,500 crore to its first integrated healthcare network in Pune, funded entirely from within the group, and aims to be present in more than 10 cities over the next 15 years. BIHS is a wholly owned subsidiary of Jamnalal Sons Pvt Ltd, an unlisted Bajaj family holding company.
 
The group's healthcare investment is pegged at ₹6,000-7,000 crore over four to five years. Bajaj did not disclose an overall investment outlay for the national expansion.
 
Even the sequencing of investments reflects a departure from the conventional hospital-centric approach. BIHS will first establish a network of medical centres, home healthcare services and ambulatory centres — facilities offering day-care surgeries, chemotherapy, dialysis and advanced diagnostics without requiring overnight hospitalisation — before commissioning its 500-bed hospital.
 
“The hospital feeds the medical centres and the ambulatory centres, not the other way around,” Bajaj said.
 
BIHS plans to establish six to nine multispecialty medical centres, at least two day surgery centres, a hospital and home healthcare services across Pune, eventually employing around 2,000 people, including doctors, nurses and allied healthcare professionals.
 
Nivara's first medical centre, spread across 12,000 sq ft at Pune's Amanora township, will open next week with more than 20 in-house specialists, followed by a second centre in a couple of months. At least two day surgery centres are expected to become operational next year. 
Construction of the hospital is expected to begin in 2027. BIHS acquired a five-acre plot within Pune Municipal Corporation limits around four months ago. By the time the hospital becomes operational, the company expects to have an established patient base and a network offering primary and specialist consultations, diagnostics, pharmacy, physiotherapy, home healthcare and day-care procedures.
 
BIHS expects to expand into multiple cities simultaneously after 2030, once it has established its Pune network. Bajaj said the company would evaluate both metros and non-metros based on their healthcare needs.
 
Acquisitions, too, are not ruled out, although the immediate priority is to establish BIHS's institutional culture across its different healthcare formats before integrating another organisation.
 
Changing the economics of healthcare
 
The commercial viability of the model will depend on BIHS's ability to generate sufficient earnings from services outside hospitals, where the nature and frequency of patient engagement would be different from those in a conventional hospital business. While the 500-bed hospital will account for a sizeable share of earnings, Bajaj expects the facilities outside it to make a substantial contribution. He declined to quantify the earnings mix, saying the company was still working with projections.
 
BIHS has set aggressive internal break-even targets, Bajaj said, without disclosing the timelines. He acknowledged, however, that the business could take somewhat longer to break even than conventional healthcare ventures, given the novelty of its model. While each facility will have its own unit economics, the company will assess profitability at an integrated healthcare system level.
 
“We build businesses for decades, not for a couple of years,” he said.
 
The model also departs from conventional practices in the way doctors are employed and incentivised. All doctors will be on the company's payroll, with their performance assessed on clinical outcomes, quality of care, patient experience and readmission rates, rather than revenue generation and patient conversion ratios. Consultations at Nivara will last a minimum of 10-12 minutes.
 
BIHS is also looking to reduce dependence on individual doctors by incorporating standardised treatment protocols and clinical pathways into its electronic medical records system. Its technology architecture comprises more than 80 applications connecting doctors, diagnostic laboratories, medical centres and patients. A single patient ID will allow medical records to be accessed across its network nationally.
 
Each patient will have a dedicated care team comprising a general physician, a nurse coach or nutritionist, and an emotional well-being coach or therapist, with specialists involved when required. The company also plans to offer allopathy, Ayurveda and homeopathy within its healthcare network.
 
Over the past few years, Bajaj and his team have studied around 35 healthcare institutions across North America, Europe and Asia. The advantage of entering healthcare through a greenfield venture, he said, was the ability to adopt global and domestic practices without the constraints of legacy systems.
 
Bringing insurers into the picture
 
A critical component of BIHS's business model will be managed care, under which patients will pay a monthly subscription for access to healthcare services, with an emphasis on preventive care, early diagnosis and continuous health management.
 
Initially, the subscription will cover outpatient services, including consultations, treatment of routine illnesses, health check-ups and specialist consultations. As its network expands, BIHS plans to extend the offering to cover the entire healthcare journey, including surgeries, under a monthly payment structure.
 
In India, where health insurance coverage remains largely centred on hospitalisation, financing outpatient and preventive care will be critical to the success of such a model.
 
Having insurance companies within the Bajaj Group gives BIHS an opportunity to develop such products. Bajaj said the group companies would, however, deal with each other at arm's length, and BIHS would also work with external insurers.
 
“Whether it is the right way or not, time will tell. But we believe that this is the way healthcare should be delivered and experienced in India,” Bajaj said.

data.title: Irdai to form working groups on real-time health claims tracking, metrics
data.description:
The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (Irdai) plans to set up two industry working groups within the next 10 days to improve transparency in health claims processing and standardise performance metrics across insurers, Chairman Ajay Seth said on Thursday.
 
Speaking at the CII Financing Summit, Seth said the working groups would be formed under the Insurance Advisory Committee (IAC), following the constitution of a sub-committee.
 
“We are in the process of forming two working groups with the industry and expect it may be in about 10 days’ time to form those industry groups,” he said.
 
One working group will examine ways to provide real-time visibility across the health insurance claims process, including pre-authorisation, hospital discharge and claim settlement. The other will work on developing standardised performance metrics for claims and grievance redressal to enable comparisons across insurers.
 
 
Questioning the industry’s reliance on claim settlement ratios, Seth said the commonly used metric, which is largely based on the number of claims decided, does not necessarily reflect the experience of policyholders. Such figures could include claims that are paid fully or partially, repudiated, rejected or closed.
 
For policyholders, the more relevant measure is whether the insurer has paid the full amount claimed, rather than simply the number of claims settled, he said.
 
Irdai wants insurers to compete on product performance, claims responsiveness and grievance redressal, backed by common definitions and disclosures.
 
Seth also flagged shortcomings in the industry’s grievance redressal mechanism, pointing out that around 60 per cent of grievances, when reconsidered by senior officials within insurance companies, are resolved in favour of policyholders. Similarly, around 60 per cent of the remaining cases taken up by insurance ombudsmen are also decided in favour of policyholders.
 
He said insurers should treat grievances as feedback to improve product design, sales practices, claims decisions and customer service, rather than merely as cases to be disposed of.
 
Seth also highlighted delays in claims processing caused by repeated requests for documentation and said insurers should communicate documentation requirements upfront to minimise subsequent queries and delays.
 
On motor insurance, he flagged the large number of pending motor accident claims before tribunals. Nearly 10 lakh cases are pending, against which insurers have created reserves of around ₹87,000 crore. Some cases date back several decades, with the oldest cited by him dating to 1989.
 
Seth also said Irdai was examining the Ayushman Bharat Health Account (ABHA) as a common identity framework for health insurance. This could help insurers improve underwriting and offer more competitive pricing, particularly when individuals move between group and individual health insurance policies, where information on their previous coverage may not be readily available.
 
On the proposed Public Insurance Registry, Seth said the initiative was intended to improve transparency around insurance products, insurers’ market conduct and distributors. He clarified that the focus was on data governance rather than creating a centralised database, with minimal centralisation of information.
 
He also called for customers to be able to access product information and pricing without having to share personal details upfront.
 
“The product is needed for the general public. It is a regulated product, but personal details are being sought before a price is given. That is not how an industry should build itself, particularly when it is talking about expanding coverage,” he said, describing the requirement as a “toll” on consumers.
 
Seth said insurance products should be accessible for comparison before customers are asked to provide personal information. He also called for plain-language summaries in local languages explaining policy coverage, exclusions and returns.
 
The proposed measures, he said, were aimed at strengthening trust in the insurance sector, with the policyholder’s experience at the time of a claim being the ultimate test of the promise made when a policy is sold.

data.title: EPFO approves systematic withdrawal plan for retiring members savings
data.description:
The retirement fund body EPFO on Thursday approved a Systematic Withdrawal Plan (SWP) for its retiring members to receive their accumulated provident fund savings in periodic instalments instead of withdrawing the entire corpus at once.
 Under the SWP, retiring members of the Employees' Provident Fund Organisation will receive their accumulated provident fund savings in periodic instalments instead of withdrawing the entire amount at once, a Labour Ministry release said.
 The decision was taken at the 240th meeting of the Central Board of Trustees (CBT) of the Employees' Provident Fund (EPF), chaired by Union Minister for Labour & Employment and Youth Affairs & Sports, Mansukh Mandaviya.
 
 The Board approved a proposal to introduce a Systematic Withdrawal Plan, enabling retiring EPF members to receive their accumulated provident fund savings in periodic instalments instead of withdrawing the entire amount at once.
 This reform will enable retiring members to withdraw their accumulated provident fund savings at regular intervals, such as monthly, quarterly or half-yearly, based on their preference.
 This facility would provide members with a structured source of periodic income while allowing the remaining corpus to continue generating returns, thereby helping augment their retirement income and supplement their pension benefits.
 The facility would be entirely voluntary, with no compulsion on members to opt for withdrawals.
 The option may also be extended to eligible family members/beneficiaries, ensuring greater flexibility and financial security for the family. This aims to ensure stable post-retirement income, reduce reinvestment risks, strengthen fund sustainability, and extend social security coverage to gig and platform workers.
 SWP will enable members to convert their retirement savings into a stable and predictable stream of systematic withdrawals post-retirement, while preserving ownership of the underlying corpus.
 Approximately 6.32 lakh EPF members aged above 55 years with provident fund accumulations exceeding Rs 5 lakh are expected to be the primary beneficiaries of the proposed SWP framework during the initial phase.

data.title: DEA secretary seeks fresh PPP push, asks industry to tackle wage stagnation
data.description:
The government is looking towards newer financing models for the infrastructure sector through a renewed focus on public-private partnerships, Economic Affairs Secretary Anuradha Thakur told industry leaders, urging the industry to address wage stagnation to stimulate demand in the economy.
 
Addressing business leaders at the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI) annual general meeting on Thursday, Thakur said the industry-government partnership on infrastructure needed to be enhanced. “Now it's time that we take our partnership forward (in) the infrastructure PPPs (and work on) what would be the road map because we don't want to slip up again, we don't want over-enthusiasm again. We want sure footing in which the industry can come in, partner, leverage government budgets and move forward in an accelerated manner,” Thakur said.
  
The DEA secretary recalled that while PPPs were accelerating earlier, around the time the National Highways Authority of India first came up, inadequately analysed traffic projections and irrational lending by banks derailed this momentum, particularly in the road sector.
 
Thakur acknowledged the industry's demand for a new development finance institution (DFI). “In our conversations we have spoken about the fact that long tenor lending for the manufacturing and project finance space is something that probably the industry is feeling the need for, that very strong banks with strong balance sheets are there. So we will look into not only the merits, but how that can be shaped up,” Thakur said, adding that three very big DFIs active earlier were wound up as they ran into some issues.
 
The DEA secretary urged business leaders to strengthen their linkages with micro, small and medium enterprises for capacity building and liquidity flows.
 
In large infrastructure projects, private developers financed and built highways while recovering their investments through toll collections during the concession period under the build-operate-transfer (BOT) toll model. A report by a committee constituted by the DEA in 2015 said several projects became unviable under this model due to lower-than-expected traffic and high construction costs, alongside excessive borrowing, a shortage of funds with developers and inadequate checks by banks before lending, leading to a slowdown in infrastructure PPP projects.
 
Consequently, later models like engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) and the hybrid annuity model (HAM) factored in traffic and revenue risks. “The government responded by…moving on to EPC (Engineering, Procurement, and Construction) contracts, and then coming up with the new HAM (Hybrid Annuity Model) model which has really put us back on firm footing in pushing our road sector,” Thakur said.
 
The central government has accounted for the bulk of infrastructure spending recently. For instance, it accounted for 49 per cent of such investments between 2019 and 2023, according to the Economic Survey 2024-25.
 
Underlining the slew of reforms that saw people move above the extreme poverty and poverty lines, Thakur urged industry leaders to address wage stagnation, holding that higher wages could stimulate demand and strengthen the virtuous cycle of economic expansion.
 
“You all need to look into that... It stimulates demand, then the virtuous cycle again steps up," she said, adding that the government, industry and communities needed to enter into a “golden handshake” with each other to accelerate economic growth.

data.title: Gamers skip work, crowd gaming cafes for GTA VI as PM Modi joins the buzz
data.description:
Jacob Joel first played Grand Theft Auto in school, then again in college. On Thursday, the 30-year-old IT professional took the day off to play GTA VI in a Bengaluru gaming cafe's mini-theater, steering a speedboat beneath a bridge on a 100-inch projection screen with surround sound.
 
"We waited around 13 long years to get into GTA VI ... that is a nostalgic feeling," Joel said, controller in hand, eyes fixed on the screen.
 
Made for an estimated $1 billion or more, "Grand Theft Auto VI" launched worldwide on Thursday to glowing early reviews, in what is billed as the most anticipated video game release in history.
 
 
In India, one of the world's largest gaming markets with an estimated 550 million players and where most gaming happens on mobile phones, the launch of "Grand Theft Auto VI" turned a console-only title into a social event. It sent players to gaming cafes, drove hours-long live streams and even drew in Prime Minister Narendra Modi, underscoring the growing appeal of premium gaming as a cultural marker.
 
Popular Indian gaming YouTubers CarryMinati and Mythpat each streamed GTA VI for about 10 hours, drawing more than 13 million views apiece by Thursday afternoon.
 
"India is playing a whole new game!" Modi wrote on X, above 10 images modelled on Grand Theft Auto artwork that compared India at the time of GTA V's 2013 release with the country today.
 
Modi has stepped up efforts to woo young voters since youth-led protests over jobs and education pushed his party to sharpen its social media outreach.
 

CAFES FILL CONSOLE GAP

 
Reuters spoke to at least a dozen gamers who crowded gaming cafes in cities including Delhi, Bengaluru and Srinagar on launch day.
 
Because GTA VI is available only on consoles, gaming cafes offered many Indian players a cheaper alternative to buying the hardware. The cafes charge as little as 250 rupees ($2.67) per hour.
 
At the Gaming Mania cafe in Delhi, players sank into tan couches with white controllers, as one complained to another that he had not yet spotted a single bike in the game.
 
Divya Gupta, 48, co-owner of the cafe, said that she had fielded 40 to 50 calls through the day, including from small children asking whether they could play. She said GTA slots were fully pre-booked through Sunday despite a slight price increase.
 
In Bengaluru, Navin Rajendran, 50, owner of the Gamineazy cafe, said the rush was about more than just playing the game.
 
"This is something people want to be seen playing. It's about the bragging rights," he said.

data.title: Realty executives flag policy gaps, regulatory hurdles in Delhi's MPD-2047
data.description:
Delays in framing detailed policies, regulatory uncertainty and the involvement of multiple government agencies were among the key challenges that needed to be addressed for the implementation of Delhi's Master Plan 2047 (MPD-2047), top real estate executives said on Thursday at an Assocham event.
 
The MPD-2047, notified by the Union government in August, estimates that Delhi will need around 4 million additional housing units by 2047, when its population is projected to reach 32 million. The plan envisages meeting this demand through redevelopment, densification, transit-oriented development and planned urban expansion, supported by adequate infrastructure.
 
While describing the plan as forward-looking, developers said the supporting rules and regulations were yet to be formulated, which could delay the planning and execution of potential projects.
  
“Three or four months after notification, how many developers have filed applications for approvals? That is the proof of the pudding. It is a good plan, but a plan cannot execute itself,” said Gaurav Jain, vice-president of Naredco and managing director of Samyak Properties and Infra.
 
Jain said that while multiple agencies were involved, they would have to undertake an interactive approach to improve the implementation of the system, starting with approvals. “The question is how we execute these policies. The DDA and other agencies responsible for implementation need to be part of this conversation,” he said.
 
Vineet Kanwar, director and chief executive of DLF, said the Centre, the state government and the municipal corporation had separate responsibilities, complicating the process for developers.
 
“The central government controls some land, the state government handles other matters, and the municipal corporation has its own responsibilities. With so many agencies, it becomes difficult for developers to navigate the system,” he said.
 
Ankur Jalan, chief executive officer of Golden Growth Fund, a Sebi-registered Category II Alternative Investment Fund (AIF), said the involvement of multiple agencies created uncertainty for investors. “Even if you own a parcel of land, you may not be able to develop it because you do not know how to obtain the required licence. Such uncertainty deters investors,” he said.
 
Sanjeev Ailawadi, head - legal at Max Estates, said the Centre, state and municipal authorities, along with other government agencies, often had overlapping roles and regulations, which needed simplification.

data.title: Yes Bank AT-1 bondholders urge RBI to prioritise investor protection
data.description:
Holders of  Yes Bank's AT-1 bonds have written to the country's central bank, urging it to prioritise investor protection after it sought a review of a Supreme Court ruling that restored these bonds last month, according to a copy of the letter reviewed by Reuters.
 
The dispute stems from Yes Bank's rescue in 2020, when authorities wrote off ₹84.15 billion worth of additional Tier-1 (AT-1) bonds, a type of security designed to absorb losses when banks run into trouble.
 
Last month, the Supreme Court ruled the write-off illegal over procedural lapses and ordered the bonds restored. However, review petitions by the bank and the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) have delayed relief for investors.
 
 
Bondholders, in their letter dated November 18, said the RBI had remained "absent" in its capacity as the regulator "responsible for protecting the interests of the investing public and the integrity of the banking system".
 
Acting on behalf of the bondholders, Axis Trustee Services Limited has separately filed a contempt petition in the Supreme Court, alleging that Yes Bank and its directors have failed to comply with court directions and have not taken any steps to restore the bonds.
 
In the contempt petition, a copy of which has been reviewed by Reuters, the trustee said bondholders, including retail investors, pension funds and provident funds, had been deprived of their investments for more than six years and still had no visibility on the restoration of the bonds and payment of coupons.
 
The trustee argued that the bank could not avoid complying with the ruling while pursuing other legal remedies because the judgment remained in force.
 
The bondholders, in their letter to the central bank, said they expected the RBI to oversee implementation of the Supreme Court verdict and protect investors rather than align itself with further challenges to the ruling.
 
The RBI and Yes Bank did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

data.title: Tata Sons board reviews Air India performance amid mounting losses
data.description:
Tata Sons board members, including Chairman N Chandrasekaran and Noel Tata, on Thursday reviewed the performance of loss-making Air India, according to sources.
 
Chandrasekaran, Noel Tata, and other board members Harish Manwani, Anita Marangoly George and Saurabh Agrawal visited the airline's headquarters and its training academy in Gurugram, they added.
 
They also visited the airline's Operations Control Centre (OCC).
 
Another board member, Venu Srinivas, was not present.
 
Air India MD and CEO Tewolde Gebremariam made a presentation on the airline's performance and plans to the board members, sources said.
 
The airline is co-owned by Tata Sons and Singapore Airlines.
 
The review by Tata Sons board members also comes a day before Air India's board meeting on Friday.
 
 
Integrating key operations of Air India and Air India Express, and plans for cost rationalisation, are likely to be discussed at the carrier's board meeting, sources said.
 
Surging fuel prices, Pakistan airspace restrictions disrupting long-haul flight operations, and other headwinds widened Air India's loss to more than ₹22,000 crore in FY26.
 
The airline, acquired by the Tatas from the government in January 2022, is in the midst of an ambitious transformation plan that has also faced hurdles, including supply chain woes hitting fleet upgradation and delaying aircraft deliveries.
 
On October 1, Ethiopian Airlines Group veteran Gebremariam took over the reins of Air India. He is the second foreigner to helm the carrier after Campbell Wilson, who stepped down earlier this year.
 
Gebremariam is focused on ways to reduce expenses and has urged Air India staff to embed a mindset of frugality and accountability in all their work. The airline has also set up a multi-disciplinary team to identify cost-saving opportunities.
 
On November 3, Gebremariam said Air India will rebalance its network, work to regain overseas market share, reduce costs and order more wide-body planes.
 
"In fact, more growth may come from the full-service (operations) wide-body (operations) because the opportunity there is much bigger.
 
"... on the LCC (Low Cost Carrier) side also, on Air India Express, there is growth. We want to position these brands to the customers of all segments in the market," he had said.
 
Meanwhile, Noel Tata has opposed Chandrasekaran's reappointment as Tata Sons Chairman on a slew of concerns, including the crucial question of its listing.
 
The financial performance of some of the bets, like the digital foray, Air India and the electronics business taken by Chandrasekaran, is also among Noel Tata's concerns.
 
On November 11, Singapore Airlines (SIA) said Air India has made tangible progress in its multi-year transformation, including enhancements to customer experience and operational performance.
 
"SIA and its partner, Tata Sons, recognise that a transformation of this scale will take time.
 
"Both partners continue to work closely to support Air India's journey towards profitable growth, including strengthening structural cost efficiencies, unlocking greater synergies between Air India and Air India Express, sharpening its commercial strategy to navigate current external challenges and elevating its customer proposition," SIA had said.
